title: The hypertrophy series: the impact of sets and reps on intensity
summary: NH explains that intensity ramps up within a set as reps accumulate and across sets as fatigue builds, so a set started at 70% can reach near-failure intensity. This fatigue must be controlled; supersets, pre-fatigue and evolving rep ranges exploit it, but programming should rely mostly on fresh percentages to avoid junk volume and overtraining.
claims: A set at 70% of 1RM is 70% only for the first rep; each following rep is effectively higher intensity
Ramping intensity across reps is why we train with sets and reps and to failure: a set started at 70% can reach around 95%
Set intensity is the average of each rep's intensity, so low-rep sets at 90% still have their place
Intensity also compounds across sets: the first rep of set two isn't really 70% because the muscle is pre-fatigued
This accumulating intensity creates muscular and structural fatigue; if you don't control it you can end up unable to return to baseline
Evolving rep ranges, pre-fatigue and supersets let you taste high intensity without excessive risk, accumulating high-quality tonnage
Unplanned pre-fatigue hinders progression; deliberately scheduled pre-fatigue feeds intensity
Some baseline abilities, like doing ten push-ups, are never lost once trained
Before the point of no return lies an overtraining zone where you can recover but the loads you can move are irrelevant
Program from fresh percentages of your true 1RM, not fatigued ones; otherwise you can always do more and end up training five hours of junk volume
Fatigue-inflated intensity should be used marginally for supersets and pre-fatigue, not as the program's foundation
